Zombie Apocalypse: Survival Choices

Anglais · Première et Terminale · lycée général et technologique, et bac pro

Zombie Apocalypse: Survival Choices

A fiction of survival, from Defoe to The Walking Dead · Anglais · Première et Terminale (lycée général et technologique), bac pro · Five lessons

1. Axe du programme

Programme d’anglais du lycée général et technologique, BO n° 22 du 29 mai 2025, en vigueur en Première et en Terminale depuis la rentrée 2026.

ClasseAxe principalAxes possibles aussi
PremièreAxe 4. Innovations scientifiques et responsabilité. Face à une infection inconnue, que doit-on dire, décider, accepter ? Le couvre-feu, l’isolement d’un ami mordu, la vérité due par les autorités (lesson 1, débat C1/C2) : la séquence pose la question de la responsabilité en temps d’épidémie, de Defoe (1722) à aujourd’hui.Axe 3. Art et pouvoir : choisir un chef, fonder une règle commune (Hobbes, Shakespeare, lesson 4). Axe 2. Diversité et inclusion : ouvrir ou non la porte à l’inconnu qui frappe (lessons 2 et 3).
TerminaleAxe 3. Fictions et réalités. Une fiction de survie (le message radio, la série The Walking Dead) relue à la lumière de textes réels ou fondateurs : la peste de Londres chez Defoe, l’état de nature chez Hobbes, le dernier homme de Mary Shelley.Axe 4. Enjeux et formes de la communication : le message d’urgence, la rumeur, la bande-annonce, la lettre d’adieu. Axe 1. Espace privé et espace public : le couvre-feu et la règle commune face aux choix intimes et à la lettre privée.
LLCER anglaisPremière : thématique « Imaginaires », axe « Utopies et dystopies » (le monde d’après), avec « Imaginaires effrayants ».Première : thématique « Rencontres », axe « Relation entre l’individu et le groupe ». Terminale : thématique « Expression et construction de soi », axe « L’expression des émotions » (la lettre d’adieu).
Bac proLe programme de langues vivantes de la voie professionnelle (BO spécial n° 5 du 11 avril 2019) n’impose pas d’axe : la séquence en travaille la dimension culturelle (une série et des textes du monde anglophone) et prépare l’oral de l’examen (prise de parole en continu à partir d’un document, puis échange).Lien possible avec la prévention santé environnement (consignes de sécurité, premiers secours) et l’enseignement moral et civique (la règle commune, l’entraide).

2. Problématique

What would you choose to survive, and how would you say goodbye? Que choisirait-on pour survivre, et comment dirait-on adieu ?

Lesson 1: What would you do in the first hour of an outbreak? · Lesson 2: What would you choose, and can you justify it? · Lesson 3: What moral dilemma does a survival series put on screen? · Lesson 4: How can a group survive together? · Lesson 5: What would you write to someone you may never see again?

Class rule: everything here is fiction. We imagine, we do not frighten. Nobody has to share personal fears.

3. Objectifs linguistiques

  • Modals of deduction and imperatives: it must be serious, it can't be a joke, stay inside (lesson 1).
  • The second conditional: If I were you, I would …; I would rather … than … (lesson 2).
  • Giving a moral opinion: should, ought to, had better, should have (lesson 3).
  • Obligation and prohibition: must, have to, mustn't, don't have to (lesson 4).
  • Past, present and future in one letter: I am writing, we arrived, I have lost, we will wait (lesson 5).
  • Activités langagières : compréhension de l’écrit (message radio, tableaux, prémisse de la série, textes de Defoe, Hobbes, Shakespeare et Mary Shelley), compréhension de l’oral (bande-annonce officielle), expression orale en continu (annonce d’urgence, présentation du plan), interaction orale (débat, conseil de survie), expression écrite (journal, choix argumenté, lettre d’adieu).

4. Ancrage culturel

Le récit d’épidémie, de Daniel Defoe (A Journal of the Plague Year, 1722) à la série The Walking Dead (AMC, 2010 à 2022, d’après la bande dessinée de Robert Kirkman, Tony Moore et Charlie Adlard) ; l’état de nature chez Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) ; l’ordre et le chef chez Shakespeare (Troilus and Cressida, le discours d’Ulysse) ; Mary Shelley, The Last Man (1826) ; la lettre d’adieu. Œuvre : Edvard Munch, Anxiety (1894). Série classée TV-MA aux États-Unis : en classe, seulement la bande-annonce officielle, visionnée d’abord par le professeur.

5. Niveau CECRL

  • Première : B1+ vers B2.
  • Terminale LV1 : B2 vers C1, avec un parcours C1/C2 à chaque lesson.
  • Bac pro (Version B) : B1, cinq lessons plus courtes.
  • Version dys : B1, cinq lessons, une étape à la fois.

Lesson 1: Day one: the outbreak

Part 1. What would you do in the first hour of an outbreak?

Objectives

  • Discover the scenario and its vocabulary
  • Make deductions with must, might, can't
  • Give a short emergency announcement

Warm-up

The teacher reads a fictional radio alert: 'Stay indoors. Do not open your door.' Students list five questions they would ask.

Documents

Class rule. Everything here is fiction. We imagine, we do not frighten. Nobody has to share personal fears.
Document 1: emergency broadcast (fiction). This is an emergency message. An unknown infection is spreading across the region. The infected become violent after a bite. A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies, and wait for instructions on this frequency.

First hour checklist

ActionWhyPriority (1 to 3)
Fill bottles with waterthe network might stop
Lock doors and windowsthe infected must not enter
Charge phones and a radioto receive news
Contact familyto agree on a meeting point

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
outbreakthe sudden start of a disease
infectedcarrying the disease
bitean attack with the teeth
sheltera safe place to stay
suppliesfood, water, medicine
hordea huge moving crowd
curfewa time when you must stay inside
rumourunchecked information

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: Day one: the outbreak

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 1 “emergency broadcast” (fiction) and the first hour checklist, with Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year (1722)

  • “An unknown infection is spreading across the region. The infected become violent after a bite.” (Document 1)
  • “A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies, and wait for instructions on this frequency.” (Document 1)
  • “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop.” (First hour checklist)
  • “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague; and though I had indeed no symptoms of that distemper, […] I was not without apprehension that I really was infected.” (Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year, 1722)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 1What strikes you first?
“An unknown infection is spreading across the region” (Document 1).
The broadcast names a danger without explaining it: we know that it spreads, not what it is. Deduction starts here: it must be serious.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 1Which clues? In which line?
“The infected become violent after a bite” (Document 1).
The radio never says “zombies”: “the infected” is a medical euphemism that sounds controlled and avoids panic.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDoc. 1What effect? What contrast?
“A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies” (Document 1) and “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop” (checklist).
Imperatives give short, clear orders; the checklist gives each action a reason with a modal of deduction.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDefoeWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: in an outbreak, people are afraid of the disease only.
Not confirmed: in 1722, Defoe writes that “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague”, and his narrator fears he is infected with “no symptoms”. Fear and rumour spread faster than the disease.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“wait for instructions on this frequency” (Document 1) and “I was not without apprehension that I really was infected” (Defoe).
In the first hour, the best choice is calm action: protect the house, collect supplies, contact the family and check the news, because panic and rumour are dangers too.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Activities

  1. Read the broadcast and underline the instructions (imperatives).
  2. Rank the checklist and justify your top priority.
  3. Deduction: the shops must be empty. The radio might stop. It can't be a joke: the army is on the roads.
  4. Oral: in pairs, record a 30 second emergency announcement for your town.

More activities

Exercises
  1. Complete with must, might or can't: The army is everywhere, so it ______ be serious.
  2. The phone network is slow; it ______ stop soon.
  3. It ______ be a film: the whole country is affected.
  4. Find two imperatives in the broadcast.
  5. Give the meaning of 'curfew'.
Answer key: exercises
  1. must
  2. might
  3. can't
  4. Stay inside, collect (also: wait)
  5. A time when you must stay inside

Lesson 2: Survival choices

Part 2. What would you choose, and can you justify it?

Objectives

  • Use second conditional (If I were..., I would...)
  • Compare options
  • Justify a decision

Warm-up

Desert island game: you can carry only three objects. Which ones and why?

Documents

Dilemma table

SituationOption AOption BYour choice and reason
A stranger knocks, asking for foodopen and sharestay silent
A friend has a small bitekeep them with the groupisolate them in a safe room
Two routesthe motorway: fast but crowdedthe forest: slow but quiet
Supplies for three dayseat normallyration to make them last a week

Object ranking table

ObjectUseScore /5
first aid kittreat wounds
torchsee at night
ropeclimb, tie
radioget news
bicyclesilent transport

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
riskpossible danger
choicea decision between options
justifygive reasons for
strangera person you do not know
sharegive part of what you have
trustbelieve someone is honest
sacrificegive up something for others
consequenceresult of an action

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Survival choices

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The dilemma table and the object ranking table, with Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), chapter XIII

  • “A stranger knocks, asking for food: open and share, or stay silent.” (Dilemma table)
  • “A friend has a small bite: keep them with the group, or isolate them in a safe room.” (Dilemma table)
  • “the motorway: fast but crowded / the forest: slow but quiet” (Dilemma table)
  • “continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.” (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651, chapter XIII)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeTableWhat strikes you first?
“A stranger knocks, asking for food”: “open and share” or “stay silent” (dilemma table).
Both options have a cost: sharing reduces the supplies, silence protects the group but abandons a person. That is a dilemma.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTableWhich clues? In which line?
“A friend has a small bite”: “keep them with the group” or “isolate them in a safe room” (dilemma table).
Isolating is not rejecting: “a safe room” protects the group and still takes care of the friend.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTableWhat effect? What contrast?
“the motorway: fast but crowded” / “the forest: slow but quiet” (dilemma table).
Antithesis: every advantage has a cost, so the choice depends on the priority, speed or safety.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictHobbesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: without rules, survivors will only fight each other.
Partly confirmed: Hobbes describes “continual fear, and danger of violent death” and a life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; but the table also offers “open and share”: cooperation is a choice too.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“ration to make them last a week” (dilemma table) and “no society” (Hobbes).
A good choice is a justified one: if I were in that situation, I would ration and share, because a group with rules lasts longer than a person alone.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 2: Survival choices · Version dys

Question: What would you choose, and can you justify it?

Four words:

  • risk: a possible danger
  • choice: a decision between options
  • justify: to give reasons for
  • stranger: a person you do not know

One line to read: “A stranger knocks, asking for food: open and share, or stay silent.” (Dilemma table)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Survival choices · Version dys

Five short steps. Read the line. Write one short idea. Then go to the next step.

Text studied: The dilemma table and the object ranking table, with Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), chapter XIII

  • “A stranger knocks, asking for food: open and share, or stay silent.” (Dilemma table)
  • “A friend has a small bite: keep them with the group, or isolate them in a safe room.” (Dilemma table)
  • “the motorway: fast but crowded / the forest: slow but quiet” (Dilemma table)
  • “continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.” (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651, chapter XIII)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeTableWhat strikes you first?
Help or hide? Both cost.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTableWhich clues? In which line?
Isolate, but take care.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTableWhat effect? What contrast?
Each route has a cost.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictHobbesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Partly: fear, but sharing too.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
Rules and sharing help us survive.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Activities

  1. Complete the dilemma table alone, then compare in groups.
  2. Grammar: If I were you, I would hide. If we shared our food, we would have less.
  3. Debate in groups of four: agree on one answer for each dilemma.
  4. Extension B2: use mixed conditionals: If we had gone earlier, we would be safe now.

More activities

Exercises
  1. If a stranger ______ (knock), I would open.
  2. If I ______ (be) the leader, I would ration food.
  3. We ______ (take) the forest route if the motorway were blocked.
  4. Give two reasons to share food.
  5. Correct: If I would have a bicycle, I would go faster.
Answer key: exercises
  1. knocked
  2. were
  3. would take
  4. to make an ally, because it is humane
  5. If I had a bicycle, I would go faster.

  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: risk, choice, justify, stranger, share, trust, sacrifice, consequence.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: risk, choice, justify, stranger, share, trust, sacrifice, consequence.
    • Every option has a ______.
    • You must make a ______.
    • Always ______ your answer.
    • A ______ knocks at the door.
    • Will you ______ your food?
    • Can we ______ him?
    • Giving up something for others is a ______.
    • Every decision has a ______.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: choose two dilemmas in the table. For each one, write your choice with “If I were …, I would …” and one reason (100 words in all).
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Table): “A stranger knocks, asking for food”: “open and share” or “stay silent” (dilemma table). Both options have a cost: sharing reduces the supplies, silence protects the group but abandons a person. That is a dilemma.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Table): “A friend has a small bite”: “keep them with the group” or “isolate them in a safe room” (dilemma table). Isolating is not rejecting: “a safe room” protects the group and still takes care of the friend.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Table): “the motorway: fast but crowded” / “the forest: slow but quiet” (dilemma table). Antithesis: every advantage has a cost, so the choice depends on the priority, speed or safety.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Hobbes): Hypothesis: without rules, survivors will only fight each other. Partly confirmed: Hobbes describes “continual fear, and danger of violent death” and a life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; but the table also offers “open and share”: cooperation is a choice too.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Both): “ration to make them last a week” (dilemma table) and “no society” (Hobbes). A good choice is a justified one: if I were in that situation, I would ration and share, because a group with rules lasts longer than a person alone.

Lesson 3: Media study: The Walking Dead

Part 3. What moral dilemma does a survival series put on screen?

Objectives

  • Understand the premise of a TV series
  • Analyse one short official extract
  • Debate and write about a moral survival dilemma

Warm-up

Students describe a TV series they know in three words. What makes a series about the end of the world popular?

Documents

Age note for the teacher. The Walking Dead is a violent series rated TV-MA in the United States. Use only the short official trailer below, watched first by the teacher; no full episodes in class.
Document: the premise. The Walking Dead is an American TV series broadcast on AMC from 31 October 2010 to November 2022, over eleven seasons. It was developed by Frank Darabont from the comic book by Robert Kirkman, Tony Moore and Charlie Adlard. Sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead. He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors.
One official extract. Watch the official Season 1 trailer on the official The Walking Dead AMC channel on YouTube or on amc.com. Teacher: pick the trailer only.

Viewing table

While watchingNotes
Places (hospital, city, road)
Sounds and music
Emotions on faces
One key image

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
premisethe starting situation of a story
comaa long state of unconsciousness
deputyan assistant to a sheriff
survivorspeople still alive
leaderthe person who guides a group
moralabout good and bad
trailera short video to advertise a film or series
dilemmaa choice between two difficult options

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Media study: The Walking Dead

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document: the premise of The Walking Dead (AMC, 2010 to 2022) and the official Season 1 trailer, with Mary Shelley, The Last Man (1826)

  • “Sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead.” (Document: the premise)
  • “He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors.” (Document: the premise)
  • “The Walking Dead” (Title of the series)
  • “I spread the whole earth out as a map before me. On no one spot of its surface could I put my finger and say, here is safety.” (Mary Shelley, The Last Man, 1826)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticePremiseWhat strikes you first?
“Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead” (premise).
The viewer discovers the disaster at the same time as Rick: we are as lost as he is.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTitleWhich clues? In which line?
The title, “The Walking Dead”, is an oxymoron.
The dead cannot walk: the title names the monsters, but also the survivors, who are alive yet losing part of their humanity.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTrailerWhat effect? What contrast?
Viewing table: “Places (hospital, city, road)”, “Sounds and music”, “Emotions on faces”.
Empty places and silence show isolation; the faces show fear and hope. The trailer sells a human story, not only monsters.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictShelleyWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the lonely survivor was invented by zombie series.
Not confirmed: in 1826, Mary Shelley's last man writes: “On no one spot of its surface could I put my finger and say, here is safety.”
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningPremiseWhich interpretation do I defend?
“He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors” (premise).
The real question is not how to fight monsters but whom to trust and help: a leader should protect the group, yet a stranger in danger needs help. The series puts that dilemma on screen.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 4: Our group survival plan

Part 4. How can a group survive together?

Objectives

  • Use obligation and prohibition (must, have to, mustn't)
  • Organise a plan with roles
  • Present the plan orally

Warm-up

Each student writes one rule for a survival camp on a sticky note. The class groups them.

Documents

Roles table

RoleMissionSkill neededName in your group
Leadertakes final decisionscalm
Medicfirst aidcare
Scoutexplores the routespeed
Cookmanages suppliesorganisation
Radio operatorcontacts other groupslistening

Plan table

StepWhereWhat we must doWhat we mustn't do
1homepack suppliesmake noise
2the routestay togethersplit up
3the shelterlock and watchwaste water

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
planan organised list of actions
routethe way you travel
rolesjobs in a group
medica person who gives first aid
scouta person who explores ahead
ruleswhat everybody must respect
mapa drawing of a place
radioa device to send messages

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 4: Our group survival plan

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The roles table and the plan table, with William Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida (about 1602), Act I, scene 3

  • “Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm.” (Roles table)
  • “What we must do: stay together. What we mustn't do: split up.” (Plan table)
  • “the shelter: lock and watch / waste water” (Plan table)
  • “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows! Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy.” (Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida, Act I, scene 3)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeRolesWhat strikes you first?
“Leader: takes final decisions”, “Medic: first aid”, “Scout: explores the route”, “Cook: manages supplies” (roles table).
Each person has one mission and one skill: the group survives because the work is shared.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesPlanWhich clues? In which line?
“What we must do: stay together” / “What we mustn't do: split up” (plan table).
Antithesis: each rule stands next to its danger, so it is easy to remember.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandPlanWhat effect? What contrast?
“1 home: pack supplies”, “2 the route: stay together”, “3 the shelter: lock and watch” (plan table).
A plan is a sequence: what we have to do changes with the place, from preparing to moving to protecting.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictUlyssesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: a group without a leader will fall apart.
Confirmed by Ulysses: “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows!” But order works only if the group accepts it: a leader needs legitimacy.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm” (roles table) and “Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy” (Shakespeare).
A group survives together with shared roles, clear rules (must, mustn't, have to) and a leader it accepts; without them, conflict follows.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 5: A farewell letter

Part 5. What would you write to someone you may never see again?

Objectives

  • Write a personal letter
  • Use the past, the present and the future
  • Express feelings and hope

Warm-up

Students listen to a calm piece of music and write three words they feel.

Documents

Model letter (fiction). Dear Sam, I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym. We arrived yesterday after two days on the road. I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes. If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring. Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave. Your friend, Alex.

Letter structure

PartContentTense
OpeningDear...none
Where I amthe situation nowpresent
What happenedthe journeypast
Memorieswhat I misspresent, past
Hopea meeting point, a promisefuture
ClosingBe brave, your friendnone

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
farewellgoodbye
memorysomething you remember
hopethe belief that things will get better
regretsadness about the past
promisesaying you will do something
loved onesthe people you love
couragebravery
goodbyethe word you say when you leave

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 5: A farewell letter

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Model letter (fiction), “Dear Sam”, with Mary Shelley, The Last Man (1826), closing pages

  • “I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym. We arrived yesterday after two days on the road.” (Model letter)
  • “I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes.” (Model letter)
  • “If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring. Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave.” (Model letter)
  • “I form no expectation of alteration for the better; but the monotonous present is intolerable to me.” (Mary Shelley, The Last Man, 1826)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeLetterWhat strikes you first?
“I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym” (model letter).
The present continuous puts the reader inside the moment; the candlelight shows that there is no electricity any more.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesLetterWhich clues? In which line?
“We arrived yesterday after two days on the road” (model letter).
Past simple with a time word: the action is finished and precise.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandLetterWhat effect? What contrast?
“I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes” (model letter).
Affectionate irony: Alex misses the “terrible” jokes; it is a tender way of saying “I loved being with you”.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLetterWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the letter is only a goodbye.
Not confirmed: “If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring.” The letter also gives a meeting point and a hope.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave” (model letter) and “the monotonous present is intolerable to me” (Shelley).
To someone you may never see again, you write where you are, what happened, what you miss and a promise: past, present and future meet in one letter, and hope answers despair.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 5: A farewell letter. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym. We arrived yesterday after two days on the road.” (Model letter)
    • “I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes.” (Model letter)
    • “If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring. Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave.” (Model letter)
    • “I form no expectation of alteration for the better; but the monotonous present is intolerable to me.” (Mary Shelley, The Last Man, 1826)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: farewell, memory, hope, regret, promise, loved ones, courage, goodbye.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: farewell, memory, hope, regret, promise, loved ones, courage, goodbye.
    • A ______ letter says goodbye.
    • A happy ______ helps you on hard days.
    • Never lose ______.
    • He feels ______ about his mistakes.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Letter): “I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym” (model letter). The present continuous puts the reader inside the moment; the candlelight shows that there is no electricity any more.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Letter): “We arrived yesterday after two days on the road” (model letter). Past simple with a time word: the action is finished and precise.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Letter): “I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes” (model letter). Affectionate irony: Alex misses the “terrible” jokes; it is a tender way of saying “I loved being with you”.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Letter): Hypothesis: the letter is only a goodbye. Not confirmed: “If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring.” The letter also gives a meeting point and a hope.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Both): “Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave” (model letter) and “the monotonous present is intolerable to me” (Shelley). To someone you may never see again, you write where you are, what happened, what you miss and a promise: past, present and future meet in one letter, and hope answers despair.

Teacher notes

A very flexible sequence. This zombie sequence is highly flexible: every lesson stands alone, lessons can be shortened, merged or reordered, and the documents can be swapped between Version A, Version B and the adapted version.

GEREX

Each lesson follows the GEREX logic: students Generate ideas (warm-up), Explore a document, Reformulate it in their own words, EXercise the language point, then reuse it in a short task. The worksheet and the homework close the loop.

Differentiated pedagogy

  • Three versions: Version A (lycée général et technologique), Version B (Bac pro), adapted version for dyslexic and neurodiverse students.
  • Sentence starters on every page for students who need support.
  • Extension tasks for strong students.
  • Role plays in pairs or small groups, with roles of different difficulty.
  • Each worksheet has a QR code so students can open it on a phone.

Lesson 1: Day one: the outbreak

Part 1. What would you do in the first hour of an outbreak?

Objectives

  • Discover the scenario and its vocabulary
  • Make deductions with must, might, can't
  • Give a short emergency announcement

Warm-up

The teacher reads a fictional radio alert: 'Stay indoors. Do not open your door.' Students list five questions they would ask.

Documents

Class rule. Everything here is fiction. We imagine, we do not frighten. Nobody has to share personal fears.
Document 1: emergency broadcast (fiction). This is an emergency message. An unknown infection is spreading across the region. The infected become violent after a bite. A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies, and wait for instructions on this frequency.

First hour checklist

ActionWhyPriority (1 to 3)
Fill bottles with waterthe network might stop
Lock doors and windowsthe infected must not enter
Charge phones and a radioto receive news
Contact familyto agree on a meeting point

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
outbreakthe sudden start of a disease
infectedcarrying the disease
bitean attack with the teeth
sheltera safe place to stay
suppliesfood, water, medicine
hordea huge moving crowd
curfewa time when you must stay inside
rumourunchecked information

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: Day one: the outbreak

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 1 “emergency broadcast” (fiction) and the first hour checklist, with Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year (1722)

  • “An unknown infection is spreading across the region. The infected become violent after a bite.” (Document 1)
  • “A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies, and wait for instructions on this frequency.” (Document 1)
  • “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop.” (First hour checklist)
  • “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague; and though I had indeed no symptoms of that distemper, […] I was not without apprehension that I really was infected.” (Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year, 1722)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 1What strikes you first?
“An unknown infection is spreading across the region” (Document 1).
The broadcast names a danger without explaining it: we know that it spreads, not what it is. Deduction starts here: it must be serious.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 1Which clues? In which line?
“The infected become violent after a bite” (Document 1).
The radio never says “zombies”: “the infected” is a medical euphemism that sounds controlled and avoids panic.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDoc. 1What effect? What contrast?
“A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies” (Document 1) and “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop” (checklist).
Imperatives give short, clear orders; the checklist gives each action a reason with a modal of deduction.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDefoeWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: in an outbreak, people are afraid of the disease only.
Not confirmed: in 1722, Defoe writes that “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague”, and his narrator fears he is infected with “no symptoms”. Fear and rumour spread faster than the disease.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“wait for instructions on this frequency” (Document 1) and “I was not without apprehension that I really was infected” (Defoe).
In the first hour, the best choice is calm action: protect the house, collect supplies, contact the family and check the news, because panic and rumour are dangers too.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Terminale LV1 · C1/C2 extension track

For strong or anglophone students. Outbreak stories are much older than zombies: literature has imagined the collapse of order for centuries.

Extended extract

It was a very ill time to be sick in, for if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague; and though I had indeed no symptoms of that distemper, yet being very ill, both in my head and in my stomach, I was not without apprehension that I really was infected.
Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year, 1722 (public domain)

Critical analysis

  1. How does Defoe show that fear spreads faster than disease?
  2. What is the effect of the first person narrator?
  3. Find modern echoes of this panic in outbreak fiction.

Nuanced vocabulary

Word or phraseMeaning and use
contagionthe spread of disease, or of an emotion
apprehensionanxious fear that something bad will happen
to quarantineto isolate to prevent spread
arguablyto present a view as defensible but open to debate
to hinge onto depend entirely on

Argued writing (C1: 300 words · C2: 400 words)

Essay: 'In outbreak stories, the real epidemic is fear.' Discuss with Defoe and one modern fiction.

Debate

Debate: Should authorities tell the whole truth at the start of a crisis? Two teams, rebuttals, a closing vote.

Lesson 2: Survival choices

Part 2. What would you choose, and can you justify it?

Objectives

  • Use second conditional (If I were..., I would...)
  • Compare options
  • Justify a decision

Warm-up

Desert island game: you can carry only three objects. Which ones and why?

Documents

Dilemma table

SituationOption AOption BYour choice and reason
A stranger knocks, asking for foodopen and sharestay silent
A friend has a small bitekeep them with the groupisolate them in a safe room
Two routesthe motorway: fast but crowdedthe forest: slow but quiet
Supplies for three dayseat normallyration to make them last a week

Object ranking table

ObjectUseScore /5
first aid kittreat wounds
torchsee at night
ropeclimb, tie
radioget news
bicyclesilent transport

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
riskpossible danger
choicea decision between options
justifygive reasons for
strangera person you do not know
sharegive part of what you have
trustbelieve someone is honest
sacrificegive up something for others
consequenceresult of an action

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Survival choices

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The dilemma table and the object ranking table, with Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), chapter XIII

  • “A stranger knocks, asking for food: open and share, or stay silent.” (Dilemma table)
  • “A friend has a small bite: keep them with the group, or isolate them in a safe room.” (Dilemma table)
  • “the motorway: fast but crowded / the forest: slow but quiet” (Dilemma table)
  • “continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.” (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651, chapter XIII)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeTableWhat strikes you first?
“A stranger knocks, asking for food”: “open and share” or “stay silent” (dilemma table).
Both options have a cost: sharing reduces the supplies, silence protects the group but abandons a person. That is a dilemma.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTableWhich clues? In which line?
“A friend has a small bite”: “keep them with the group” or “isolate them in a safe room” (dilemma table).
Isolating is not rejecting: “a safe room” protects the group and still takes care of the friend.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTableWhat effect? What contrast?
“the motorway: fast but crowded” / “the forest: slow but quiet” (dilemma table).
Antithesis: every advantage has a cost, so the choice depends on the priority, speed or safety.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictHobbesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: without rules, survivors will only fight each other.
Partly confirmed: Hobbes describes “continual fear, and danger of violent death” and a life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; but the table also offers “open and share”: cooperation is a choice too.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“ration to make them last a week” (dilemma table) and “no society” (Hobbes).
A good choice is a justified one: if I were in that situation, I would ration and share, because a group with rules lasts longer than a person alone.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

4 J’anticipe · I predictHobbesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Partly: fear, but sharing too.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
Rules and sharing help us survive.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Activities

  1. Complete the dilemma table alone, then compare in groups.
  2. Grammar: If I were you, I would hide. If we shared our food, we would have less.
  3. Debate in groups of four: agree on one answer for each dilemma.
  4. Extension B2: use mixed conditionals: If we had gone earlier, we would be safe now.

Terminale LV1 · C1/C2 extension track

For strong or anglophone students. Survival choices are tested against political philosophy.

Extended extract

In such condition there is no place for industry, because the fruit thereof is uncertain; and consequently no culture of the earth; no arts; no letters; no society; and which is worst of all, continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651, chapter XIII (public domain)

Critical analysis

  1. What does Hobbes mean by 'such condition'?
  2. Why does the list end on 'short'? Analyse the rhythm.
  3. Do zombie stories confirm or contradict Hobbes?

Nuanced vocabulary

Word or phraseMeaning and use
state of naturelife before any government or law
social contractthe agreement by which people accept rules for safety
brutishsavage, like an animal
arguablyto present a view as defensible but open to debate
to hinge onto depend entirely on

Argued writing (C1: 300 words · C2: 400 words)

Argued essay: 'Without law, people become their own worst enemies.' Do survival fictions vindicate Hobbes?

Debate

Moral dilemma council: each group must defend one hard choice (share or keep, stay or leave) with a philosophical argument.

L’élève ne peut pas venir en classe ou est hospitalisé

Lesson 2: Survival choices. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “A stranger knocks, asking for food: open and share, or stay silent.” (Dilemma table)
    • “A friend has a small bite: keep them with the group, or isolate them in a safe room.” (Dilemma table)
    • “the motorway: fast but crowded / the forest: slow but quiet” (Dilemma table)
    • “continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.” (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651, chapter XIII)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: risk, choice, justify, stranger, share, trust, sacrifice, consequence.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: risk, choice, justify, stranger, share, trust, sacrifice, consequence.
    • Every option has a ______.
    • You must make a ______.
    • Always ______ your answer.
    • A ______ knocks at the door.
    • Will you ______ your food?
    • Can we ______ him?
    • Giving up something for others is a ______.
    • Every decision has a ______.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: choose two dilemmas in the table. For each one, write your choice with “If I were …, I would …” and one reason (100 words in all).
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Table): “A stranger knocks, asking for food”: “open and share” or “stay silent” (dilemma table). Both options have a cost: sharing reduces the supplies, silence protects the group but abandons a person. That is a dilemma.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Table): “A friend has a small bite”: “keep them with the group” or “isolate them in a safe room” (dilemma table). Isolating is not rejecting: “a safe room” protects the group and still takes care of the friend.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Table): “the motorway: fast but crowded” / “the forest: slow but quiet” (dilemma table). Antithesis: every advantage has a cost, so the choice depends on the priority, speed or safety.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Hobbes): Hypothesis: without rules, survivors will only fight each other. Partly confirmed: Hobbes describes “continual fear, and danger of violent death” and a life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; but the table also offers “open and share”: cooperation is a choice too.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Both): “ration to make them last a week” (dilemma table) and “no society” (Hobbes). A good choice is a justified one: if I were in that situation, I would ration and share, because a group with rules lasts longer than a person alone.

  2. choice
  3. justify
  4. stranger
  5. share
  6. trust
  7. sacrifice
  8. consequence

Lesson 3: Media study: The Walking Dead

Part 3. What moral dilemma does a survival series put on screen?

Objectives

  • Understand the premise of a TV series
  • Analyse one short official extract
  • Debate and write about a moral survival dilemma

Warm-up

Students describe a TV series they know in three words. What makes a series about the end of the world popular?

Documents

Age note for the teacher. The Walking Dead is a violent series rated TV-MA in the United States. Use only the short official trailer below, watched first by the teacher; no full episodes in class.
Document: the premise. The Walking Dead is an American TV series broadcast on AMC from 31 October 2010 to November 2022, over eleven seasons. It was developed by Frank Darabont from the comic book by Robert Kirkman, Tony Moore and Charlie Adlard. Sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead. He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors.
One official extract. Watch the official Season 1 trailer on the official The Walking Dead AMC channel on YouTube or on amc.com. Teacher: pick the trailer only.

Viewing table

While watchingNotes
Places (hospital, city, road)
Sounds and music
Emotions on faces
One key image

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
premisethe starting situation of a story
comaa long state of unconsciousness
deputyan assistant to a sheriff
survivorspeople still alive
leaderthe person who guides a group
moralabout good and bad
trailera short video to advertise a film or series
dilemmaa choice between two difficult options

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Media study: The Walking Dead

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document: the premise of The Walking Dead (AMC, 2010 to 2022) and the official Season 1 trailer, with Mary Shelley, The Last Man (1826)

  • “Sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead.” (Document: the premise)
  • “He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors.” (Document: the premise)
  • “The Walking Dead” (Title of the series)
  • “I spread the whole earth out as a map before me. On no one spot of its surface could I put my finger and say, here is safety.” (Mary Shelley, The Last Man, 1826)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticePremiseWhat strikes you first?
“Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead” (premise).
The viewer discovers the disaster at the same time as Rick: we are as lost as he is.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTitleWhich clues? In which line?
The title, “The Walking Dead”, is an oxymoron.
The dead cannot walk: the title names the monsters, but also the survivors, who are alive yet losing part of their humanity.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTrailerWhat effect? What contrast?
Viewing table: “Places (hospital, city, road)”, “Sounds and music”, “Emotions on faces”.
Empty places and silence show isolation; the faces show fear and hope. The trailer sells a human story, not only monsters.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictShelleyWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the lonely survivor was invented by zombie series.
Not confirmed: in 1826, Mary Shelley's last man writes: “On no one spot of its surface could I put my finger and say, here is safety.”
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningPremiseWhich interpretation do I defend?
“He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors” (premise).
The real question is not how to fight monsters but whom to trust and help: a leader should protect the group, yet a stranger in danger needs help. The series puts that dilemma on screen.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 4: Our group survival plan

Part 4. How can a group survive together?

Objectives

  • Use obligation and prohibition (must, have to, mustn't)
  • Organise a plan with roles
  • Present the plan orally

Warm-up

Each student writes one rule for a survival camp on a sticky note. The class groups them.

Documents

Roles table

RoleMissionSkill neededName in your group
Leadertakes final decisionscalm
Medicfirst aidcare
Scoutexplores the routespeed
Cookmanages suppliesorganisation
Radio operatorcontacts other groupslistening

Plan table

StepWhereWhat we must doWhat we mustn't do
1homepack suppliesmake noise
2the routestay togethersplit up
3the shelterlock and watchwaste water

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
planan organised list of actions
routethe way you travel
rolesjobs in a group
medica person who gives first aid

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 4: Our group survival plan

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The roles table and the plan table, with William Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida (about 1602), Act I, scene 3

  • “Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm.” (Roles table)
  • “What we must do: stay together. What we mustn't do: split up.” (Plan table)
  • “the shelter: lock and watch / waste water” (Plan table)
  • “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows! Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy.” (Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida, Act I, scene 3)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeRolesWhat strikes you first?
“Leader: takes final decisions”, “Medic: first aid”, “Scout: explores the route”, “Cook: manages supplies” (roles table).
Each person has one mission and one skill: the group survives because the work is shared.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesPlanWhich clues? In which line?
“What we must do: stay together” / “What we mustn't do: split up” (plan table).
Antithesis: each rule stands next to its danger, so it is easy to remember.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandPlanWhat effect? What contrast?
“1 home: pack supplies”, “2 the route: stay together”, “3 the shelter: lock and watch” (plan table).
A plan is a sequence: what we have to do changes with the place, from preparing to moving to protecting.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictUlyssesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: a group without a leader will fall apart.
Confirmed by Ulysses: “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows!” But order works only if the group accepts it: a leader needs legitimacy.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm” (roles table) and “Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy” (Shakespeare).
A group survives together with shared roles, clear rules (must, mustn't, have to) and a leader it accepts; without them, conflict follows.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

    • We need a clear ______.
    • The scout checks the ______.
    • Each member has a role: we share the ______.
    • The ______ treats wounds.
    • The ______ explores first.
    • Everybody respects the ______.
    • We draw a ______.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Roles): “Leader: takes final decisions”, “Medic: first aid”, “Scout: explores the route”, “Cook: manages supplies” (roles table). Each person has one mission and one skill: the group survives because the work is shared.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Plan): “What we must do: stay together” / “What we mustn't do: split up” (plan table). Antithesis: each rule stands next to its danger, so it is easy to remember.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Plan): “1 home: pack supplies”, “2 the route: stay together”, “3 the shelter: lock and watch” (plan table). A plan is a sequence: what we have to do changes with the place, from preparing to moving to protecting.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Ulysses): Hypothesis: a group without a leader will fall apart. Confirmed by Ulysses: “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows!” But order works only if the group accepts it: a leader needs legitimacy.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Both): “Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm” (roles table) and “Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy” (Shakespeare). A group survives together with shared roles, clear rules (must, mustn't, have to) and a leader it accepts; without them, conflict follows.

Lesson 5: A farewell letter

Part 5. What would you write to someone you may never see again?

Objectives

  • Write a personal letter
  • Use the past, the present and the future
  • Express feelings and hope

Warm-up

Students listen to a calm piece of music and write three words they feel.

Documents

Model letter (fiction). Dear Sam, I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym. We arrived yesterday after two days on the road. I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes. If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring. Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave. Your friend, Alex.

Letter structure

PartContentTense
OpeningDear...none
Where I amthe situation nowpresent
What happenedthe journeypast
Memorieswhat I misspresent, past
Hopea meeting point, a promisefuture
ClosingBe brave, your friendnone

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
farewellgoodbye
memorysomething you remember
hopethe belief that things will get better
regretsadness about the past
promisesaying you will do something
loved onesthe people you love
couragebravery
goodbyethe word you say when you leave

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 5: A farewell letter

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Model letter (fiction), “Dear Sam”, with Mary Shelley, The Last Man (1826), closing pages

  • “I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym. We arrived yesterday after two days on the road.” (Model letter)
  • “I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes.” (Model letter)
  • “If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring. Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave.” (Model letter)
  • “I form no expectation of alteration for the better; but the monotonous present is intolerable to me.” (Mary Shelley, The Last Man, 1826)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeLetterWhat strikes you first?
“I am writing this by candlelight in the old school gym” (model letter).
The present continuous puts the reader inside the moment; the candlelight shows that there is no electricity any more.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesLetterWhich clues? In which line?
“We arrived yesterday after two days on the road” (model letter).
Past simple with a time word: the action is finished and precise.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandLetterWhat effect? What contrast?
“I miss our long walks and your terrible jokes” (model letter).
Affectionate irony: Alex misses the “terrible” jokes; it is a tender way of saying “I loved being with you”.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLetterWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the letter is only a goodbye.
Not confirmed: “If you find this letter, go north to the lake: we will wait there until spring.” The letter also gives a meeting point and a hope.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Be brave” (model letter) and “the monotonous present is intolerable to me” (Shelley).
To someone you may never see again, you write where you are, what happened, what you miss and a promise: past, present and future meet in one letter, and hope answers despair.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Teacher notes

A very flexible sequence. This zombie sequence is highly flexible: every lesson stands alone, lessons can be shortened, merged or reordered, and the documents can be swapped between Version A, Version B and the adapted version.

GEREX

Each lesson follows the GEREX logic: students Generate ideas (warm-up), Explore a document, Reformulate it in their own words, EXercise the language point, then reuse it in a short task. The worksheet and the homework close the loop.

Differentiated pedagogy

  • Three versions: Version A (lycée général et technologique), Version B (Bac pro), adapted version for dyslexic and neurodiverse students.
  • Sentence starters on every page for students who need support.
  • Extension tasks for strong students.
  • Role plays in pairs or small groups, with roles of different difficulty.
  • Each worksheet has a QR code so students can open it on a phone.

Lesson 1: Day one: the outbreak

Part 1. What would you do in the first hour of an outbreak?

Objectives

  • Discover the scenario and its vocabulary
  • Make deductions with must, might, can't
  • Give a short emergency announcement

Warm-up

The teacher reads a fictional radio alert: 'Stay indoors. Do not open your door.' Students list five questions they would ask.

Documents

Class rule. Everything here is fiction. We imagine, we do not frighten. Nobody has to share personal fears.
Document 1: emergency broadcast (fiction). This is an emergency message. An unknown infection is spreading across the region. The infected become violent after a bite. A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies, and wait for instructions on this frequency.

First hour checklist

ActionWhyPriority (1 to 3)
Fill bottles with waterthe network might stop
Lock doors and windowsthe infected must not enter
Charge phones and a radioto receive news
Contact familyto agree on a meeting point

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
outbreakthe sudden start of a disease
infectedcarrying the disease
bitean attack with the teeth
sheltera safe place to stay
suppliesfood, water, medicine
hordea huge moving crowd
curfewa time when you must stay inside
rumourunchecked information

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: Day one: the outbreak

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 1 “emergency broadcast” (fiction) and the first hour checklist, with Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year (1722)

  • “An unknown infection is spreading across the region. The infected become violent after a bite.” (Document 1)
  • “A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies, and wait for instructions on this frequency.” (Document 1)
  • “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop.” (First hour checklist)
  • “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague; and though I had indeed no symptoms of that distemper, […] I was not without apprehension that I really was infected.” (Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year, 1722)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 1What strikes you first?
“An unknown infection is spreading across the region” (Document 1).
The broadcast names a danger without explaining it: we know that it spreads, not what it is. Deduction starts here: it must be serious.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 1Which clues? In which line?
“The infected become violent after a bite” (Document 1).
The radio never says “zombies”: “the infected” is a medical euphemism that sounds controlled and avoids panic.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDoc. 1What effect? What contrast?
“A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies” (Document 1) and “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop” (checklist).
Imperatives give short, clear orders; the checklist gives each action a reason with a modal of deduction.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDefoeWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: in an outbreak, people are afraid of the disease only.
Not confirmed: in 1722, Defoe writes that “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague”, and his narrator fears he is infected with “no symptoms”. Fear and rumour spread faster than the disease.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“wait for instructions on this frequency” (Document 1) and “I was not without apprehension that I really was infected” (Defoe).
In the first hour, the best choice is calm action: protect the house, collect supplies, contact the family and check the news, because panic and rumour are dangers too.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

    • “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague; and though I had indeed no symptoms of that distemper, […] I was not without apprehension that I really was infected.” (Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year, 1722)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: outbreak, infected, bite, shelter, supplies, horde, curfew, rumour.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: outbreak, infected, bite, shelter, supplies, horde, curfew, rumour.
    • There is an ______ in the region.
    • The ______ become violent.
    • The disease spreads with a ______.
    • We need a safe ______.
    • Collect water and ______.
    • A ______ of infected people is coming.
    • The ______ starts at 6 pm.
    • Do not believe every ______.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: read Document 1 and the checklist. Write your first hour diary entry (100 words): three things you do, and three modals of deduction (must, might, can't).
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Doc. 1): “An unknown infection is spreading across the region” (Document 1). The broadcast names a danger without explaining it: we know that it spreads, not what it is. Deduction starts here: it must be serious.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Doc. 1): “The infected become violent after a bite” (Document 1). The radio never says “zombies”: “the infected” is a medical euphemism that sounds controlled and avoids panic.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Doc. 1): “A curfew starts at 6 pm. Stay inside, collect water and supplies” (Document 1) and “Fill bottles with water: the network might stop” (checklist). Imperatives give short, clear orders; the checklist gives each action a reason with a modal of deduction.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Defoe): Hypothesis: in an outbreak, people are afraid of the disease only. Not confirmed: in 1722, Defoe writes that “if any one complained, it was immediately said he had the plague”, and his narrator fears he is infected with “no symptoms”. Fear and rumour spread faster than the disease.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Both): “wait for instructions on this frequency” (Document 1) and “I was not without apprehension that I really was infected” (Defoe). In the first hour, the best choice is calm action: protect the house, collect supplies, contact the family and check the news, because panic and rumour are dangers too.

Part 2. What would you choose, and can you justify it?

Objectives

Warm-up

Desert island game: you can carry only three objects. Which ones and why?

Documents

Dilemma table

SituationOption AOption BYour choice and reason
A stranger knocks, asking for foodopen and sharestay silent
A friend has a small bitekeep them with the groupisolate them in a safe room
Two routesthe motorway: fast but crowdedthe forest: slow but quiet
Supplies for three dayseat normallyration to make them last a week

Object ranking table

ObjectUseScore /5
first aid kittreat wounds
torchsee at night
ropeclimb, tie
radioget news
bicyclesilent transport

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
riskpossible danger
choicea decision between options
justifygive reasons for
strangera person you do not know
sharegive part of what you have
trustbelieve someone is honest
sacrificegive up something for others
consequenceresult of an action

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Survival choices

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The dilemma table and the object ranking table, with Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), chapter XIII

  • “A stranger knocks, asking for food: open and share, or stay silent.” (Dilemma table)
  • “A friend has a small bite: keep them with the group, or isolate them in a safe room.” (Dilemma table)
  • “the motorway: fast but crowded / the forest: slow but quiet” (Dilemma table)
  • “continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.” (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651, chapter XIII)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeTableWhat strikes you first?
“A stranger knocks, asking for food”: “open and share” or “stay silent” (dilemma table).
Both options have a cost: sharing reduces the supplies, silence protects the group but abandons a person. That is a dilemma.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTableWhich clues? In which line?
“A friend has a small bite”: “keep them with the group” or “isolate them in a safe room” (dilemma table).
Isolating is not rejecting: “a safe room” protects the group and still takes care of the friend.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTableWhat effect? What contrast?
“the motorway: fast but crowded” / “the forest: slow but quiet” (dilemma table).
Antithesis: every advantage has a cost, so the choice depends on the priority, speed or safety.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictHobbesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: without rules, survivors will only fight each other.
Partly confirmed: Hobbes describes “continual fear, and danger of violent death” and a life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; but the table also offers “open and share”: cooperation is a choice too.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“ration to make them last a week” (dilemma table) and “no society” (Hobbes).
A good choice is a justified one: if I were in that situation, I would ration and share, because a group with rules lasts longer than a person alone.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 3: Media study: The Walking Dead

Part 3. What moral dilemma does a survival series put on screen?

Objectives

  • Understand the premise of a TV series
  • Analyse one short official extract
  • Debate and write about a moral survival dilemma

Warm-up

Students describe a TV series they know in three words. What makes a series about the end of the world popular?

Documents

Age note for the teacher. The Walking Dead is a violent series rated TV-MA in the United States. Use only the short official trailer below, watched first by the teacher; no full episodes in class.
Document: the premise. The Walking Dead is an American TV series broadcast on AMC from 31 October 2010 to November 2022, over eleven seasons. It was developed by Frank Darabont from the comic book by Robert Kirkman, Tony Moore and Charlie Adlard. Sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead. He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors.
One official extract. Watch the official Season 1 trailer on the official The Walking Dead AMC channel on YouTube or on amc.com. Teacher: pick the trailer only.

Viewing table

While watchingNotes
Places (hospital, city, road)
Sounds and music
Emotions on faces
One key image

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
premisethe starting situation of a story
comaa long state of unconsciousness
deputyan assistant to a sheriff
survivorspeople still alive
leaderthe person who guides a group
moralabout good and bad
trailera short video to advertise a film or series
dilemmaa choice between two difficult options

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Media study: The Walking Dead

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document: the premise of The Walking Dead (AMC, 2010 to 2022) and the official Season 1 trailer, with Mary Shelley, The Last Man (1826)

  • “Sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead.” (Document: the premise)
  • “He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors.” (Document: the premise)
  • “The Walking Dead” (Title of the series)
  • “I spread the whole earth out as a map before me. On no one spot of its surface could I put my finger and say, here is safety.” (Mary Shelley, The Last Man, 1826)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticePremiseWhat strikes you first?
“Rick Grimes wakes up from a coma in a hospital and discovers a world overrun by the dead” (premise).
The viewer discovers the disaster at the same time as Rick: we are as lost as he is.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTitleWhich clues? In which line?
The title, “The Walking Dead”, is an oxymoron.
The dead cannot walk: the title names the monsters, but also the survivors, who are alive yet losing part of their humanity.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTrailerWhat effect? What contrast?
Viewing table: “Places (hospital, city, road)”, “Sounds and music”, “Emotions on faces”.
Empty places and silence show isolation; the faces show fear and hope. The trailer sells a human story, not only monsters.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictShelleyWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the lonely survivor was invented by zombie series.
Not confirmed: in 1826, Mary Shelley's last man writes: “On no one spot of its surface could I put my finger and say, here is safety.”
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningPremiseWhich interpretation do I defend?
“He searches for his wife and son and joins a group of survivors” (premise).
The real question is not how to fight monsters but whom to trust and help: a leader should protect the group, yet a stranger in danger needs help. The series puts that dilemma on screen.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Document … (or in the table). This shows me … because …”

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 4: Our group survival plan

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The roles table and the plan table, with William Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida (about 1602), Act I, scene 3

  • “Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm.” (Roles table)
  • “What we must do: stay together. What we mustn't do: split up.” (Plan table)
  • “the shelter: lock and watch / waste water” (Plan table)
  • “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows! Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy.” (Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida, Act I, scene 3)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeRolesWhat strikes you first?
“Leader: takes final decisions”, “Medic: first aid”, “Scout: explores the route”, “Cook: manages supplies” (roles table).
Each person has one mission and one skill: the group survives because the work is shared.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesPlanWhich clues? In which line?
“What we must do: stay together” / “What we mustn't do: split up” (plan table).
Antithesis: each rule stands next to its danger, so it is easy to remember.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandPlanWhat effect? What contrast?
“1 home: pack supplies”, “2 the route: stay together”, “3 the shelter: lock and watch” (plan table).
A plan is a sequence: what we have to do changes with the place, from preparing to moving to protecting.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictUlyssesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: a group without a leader will fall apart.
Confirmed by Ulysses: “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows!” But order works only if the group accepts it: a leader needs legitimacy.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm” (roles table) and “Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy” (Shakespeare).
A group survives together with shared roles, clear rules (must, mustn't, have to) and a leader it accepts; without them, conflict follows.
Link the analysis to the key question.

    • “the shelter: lock and watch / waste water” (Plan table)
    • “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows! Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy.” (Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida, Act I, scene 3)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: plan, route, roles, medic, scout, rules, map, radio.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: plan, route, roles, medic, scout, rules, map, radio.
    • We need a clear ______.
    • The scout checks the ______.
    • Each member has a role: we share the ______.

    • The ______ explores first.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Roles): “Leader: takes final decisions”, “Medic: first aid”, “Scout: explores the route”, “Cook: manages supplies” (roles table). Each person has one mission and one skill: the group survives because the work is shared.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Plan): “What we must do: stay together” / “What we mustn't do: split up” (plan table). Antithesis: each rule stands next to its danger, so it is easy to remember.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Plan): “1 home: pack supplies”, “2 the route: stay together”, “3 the shelter: lock and watch” (plan table). A plan is a sequence: what we have to do changes with the place, from preparing to moving to protecting.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Ulysses): Hypothesis: a group without a leader will fall apart. Confirmed by Ulysses: “Take but degree away, untune that string, And, hark, what discord follows!” But order works only if the group accepts it: a leader needs legitimacy.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Both): “Leader: takes final decisions. Skill needed: calm” (roles table) and “Each thing meets In mere oppugnancy” (Shakespeare). A group survives together with shared roles, clear rules (must, mustn't, have to) and a leader it accepts; without them, conflict follows.
